nameStory: The red morning glory gets its name from its brilliant scarlet-red flowers that open with the morning sun, just like other morning glories. It's also called 'redstar' because of the distinctive star-like shape its five-petaled flowers make when fully opened.
description: Red morning glory is a climbing annual vine that twines its way up fences, shrubs, and other plants using its flexible stems. The plant produces heart-shaped leaves and stunning bright red trumpet-shaped flowers that are much smaller than typical morning glories. This vigorous climber can reach several feet in length during the growing season, creating cascades of scarlet blooms that attract hummingbirds and butterflies.

idTips.label: Flowers
idTips.description: Small bright red trumpet-shaped flowers, about half an inch across, with five petals that form a perfect star when viewed from above - much smaller than other morning glories

idTips.label: Leaves
idTips.description: Heart-shaped leaves with smooth edges and a soft, slightly fuzzy texture when rubbed between your fingers

idTips.label: Growth Habit
idTips.description: Slender twining vine that spirals counterclockwise around supports, with stems that feel smooth and slightly succulent when gently squeezed

idTips.label: Seeds
idTips.description: Small dark brown to black seeds contained in papery capsules that rattle when shaken when mature

habitat: Red morning glory is extremely rare in New England, with only two recorded observations. When found, it typically grows in disturbed soils, garden edges, and waste places where it can climb on fences or other vegetation. It prefers sunny locations with well-drained soil.

seasonality.spring: Seeds germinate after the last frost, and young heart-shaped leaves begin appearing on slender climbing stems in late spring.
seasonality.summer: Bright red star-shaped flowers bloom continuously through summer, opening in the morning and often closing by afternoon on hot days.
seasonality.fall: Flowering continues into early fall until the first frost kills the annual vine, leaving behind small seed capsules.
seasonality.winter: No above-ground parts survive winter - only seeds remain to potentially germinate the following spring.

funFact: Despite being called 'morning glory,' the red morning glory's tiny flowers often stay open longer during the day than their larger cousins, sometimes remaining open until evening to catch the attention of late-day pollinators like hummingbirds.
confusionNotes: The small red flowers and heart-shaped leaves make this species quite distinctive among morning glories. Cardinal flower has similar red coloring but grows upright with completely different flower structure, while scarlet runner bean has red flowers but distinctive three-part compound leaves.
contextualKnowledge: This species is sometimes called 'Mexican morning glory,' but this name is ambiguous and used for several different red-flowered Ipomoea species. With only two observations recorded in New England, this is one of our region's rarest morning glories.
compareHints: Red morning glory stands out from other New England morning glories primarily by its small size and brilliant red color - most others have much larger purple, blue, or white flowers. While ivy-leaved morning glory can have reddish flowers, they're typically more purple-red and the leaves are three-lobed rather than heart-shaped.

relatedSpecies.distinction: Common morning-glory has the largest flowers among New England's morning-glories, with those distinctive heart-shaped leaves that lack the three-lobed structure of ivy-leaved morning-glory.

Among New England morning-glories, ivy-leaved is distinguished by its three-lobed leaves - common morning-glory has unlobed heart-shaped leaves, while white morning-glory has much smaller flowers and often heart-shaped but sometimes three-lobed leaves.

Garden Morning Glory stands out from its Ipomoea cousins with its large flower size and vibrant blue color range - Common Morning Glory has smaller, more purple-pink flowers, while Ivy-leaved Morning Glory has distinctly lobed leaves rather than the simple heart shape.
Cypress vine is instantly distinguished from all other morning glories by its incredibly fine, thread-like leaf segments - every other morning glory in New England has broad, solid leaves.

Among its morning glory relatives, moonflower stands out for its exclusively nighttime blooming and pure white color - most other Ipomoea species bloom during the day in shades of purple, blue, pink, or red.
Unlike its morning glory relatives that are primarily grown for their showy trumpet flowers, sweet potato is grown for foliage and edible tubers, rarely flowering in New England's climate.
Among New England morning-glories, wild potato vine stands out with its pure white flowers that have pink throats, while most others have purple, blue, or pink flowers.

Among New England morning glories, scarlet creeper is the only one with consistently bright red flowers - common morning glory has purple flowers, ivy-leaved morning glory has blue to purple blooms, and moonflower has large white flowers.

White morning-glory stands out from its Ipomoea relatives by having the smallest flowers in the genus - much tinier than the dinner-plate-sized blooms of moonflower or the vibrant purple trumpets of common morning-glory.
